scope.flow: sUSDM ERC-4626 share-token decimals() reporting to external integrators, and amounts those integrators derive/scale from the reported value
scope.environment: EVM mainnet; Solidity sUSDM token built on OpenZeppelin ERC-4626 v5.x

entities.name: External integrator (wallet, indexer, router, aggregator, oracle adapter)
User relying on share amounts and UI

statements.text: sUSDM._decimalsOffset() returns 6, enabling the OZ ERC-4626 virtual-shares mechanism at 10**6
The contract relies on OZ ERC-4626 v5.x conversion functions whose share/asset math incorporates 10**_decimalsOffset()
An external integrator, user-facing system, or price adapter queries decimals() and treats shares as a 6-decimal token when scaling values
The decimals() override returning 6 contradicts the OZ ERC-4626 implementation assumptions, under which the vault decimals are computed as USDM decimals (6) plus _decimalsOffset() (6) = 12
Following the decimals() query, the external integrator/user-facing system computes share pricing, exchange rates, minOut/maxIn, or scaled amounts using the reported share decimals
Integrators computing price-per-share, exchange rates, or minOut/maxIn from the reported 6 share decimals obtain incorrect quote values

Vault routers and aggregators that normalize to decimals() pass wrongly-scaled amounts, causing unexpected deposit/mint failures, wrong slippage protections, or misleading UI amounts that lead users to sign unintended transactions

The ERC-4626 share token should report decimals() consistent with its offset-based implementation, i.e., assetDecimals + _decimalsOffset() (12 for sUSDM), so off-chain and contract-side decimal semantics agree
The claimed victims arise only when an external party actually calls decimals() and derives or scales amounts from the returned 6-decimal value

ambiguities: No explicit report statement that decimals() can be called by anyone or is externally triggerable without authorization; that is only inferred from the ERC-4626 interface, so no such precondition is asserted.

The report provides no actor or exploit chain demonstrating a real transaction or verified loss; the failing behavior is asserted as a potential consequence of integrator scaling, not as an observed incident.

The direction and magnitude of the mis-scaling is not stated (e.g., whether 6-decimal normalization under- or over-scales against the 12-decimal internal math) and depends on which external system is used.
The report does not state that sUSDM's own core deposit/mint conversion flows are broken on-chain; it only claims off-chain/integrator misreporting, so on-chain protocol breakage remains unsupported.
